 Which EVs Have the Most Recalls in 2026
 Looking to buy an electric vehicle? Learn which models top the recall list and how to navigate safety issues before making the switch.
By
 Sean Jackson 
Edited by
 Alexandra Svokos 
Published
5 November 2026
In

 People who own electric vehicles seem to love them. Rick Wilmer, CEO of ChargePoint , told Kiplinger that EV owners have a 90% retention rate, indicating that once they switch to an EV, they don't switch back.
 With painful prices at the pump, it's no wonder buyers are making the switch. In fact, Autoblog reports that used EVs are now flying off lots faster than traditional gas vehicles. Ready to make the jump? The real challenge is narrowing down which EV best fits your lifestyle and budget.
 This is where its recall history comes into play, as it can help you spot potential issues, since the last thing you want is to spend ample time doing software updates or visiting your dealership. With this in mind, here are the EVs with the most recalls.

 The EVs with the most recalls
 (Image credit: Getty Images) Rerev examined over 50 electric models sold in the U.S. to identify those with the most safety recalls in 2026. Using recall data from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA), the report counted how many separate recalls each model had, how many cars each recall covered and how many complaints were filed.

 Understanding the most common EV recalls
 Let's start with the Tesla Model Y , which leads the list with five recalls this year. The recalls haven't been too severe. One was for headlights that were too bright, and another was for a missing certification label. Many of Tesla 's fixes are over-the-air updates, so pay close attention to software updates and comply as they arrive.
 Meanwhile, the Lucid Air arguably had the most concerning recall: It involved a fire hazard due to faulty lighting-circuit software. It was so serious that Lucid recommended drivers park their vehicles outside until the over-the-air update applied.
 Another vehicle notable for recalls is the Rivian R1S . These recalls affected everyday performance, such as a message appearing on the screen when drivers tried to view their rear cameras. There were also recalls for seat belts and front turn signals that were working improperly.
 (Image credit: Getty Images) Last but certainly not least is the Hyundai Ioniq 5 . It had 610 complaints filed with the NHTSA, the second-highest number of complaints behind the Tesla Model Y with 787. Why so many? Ioniq 5 owners have experienced a litany of issues, including power loss from integrated charging control unit failures and improperly tightened battery bus bars, creating a fire risk.
 With these trends in mind, if you're looking to buy an EV, pay close attention to recalls, as they can be a preview of future experiences.
 And if you are an EV owner, here's how to handle recalls:
 Use the NHTSA recall lookup tool by providing your car's VIN or license plate to find any outstanding recalls
 Look for over-the-air software updates and install safety patches immediately
 If you receive a recall notice, contact your dealer to schedule the free repairs
 Adhere to temporary safety precautions (such as parking outside or adjusting charging limits if advised for battery/fire risks) until the repair is completed
 Retain service documentation and verify that the recall is marked resolved in official records
 Overall, EVs offer a range of benefits that make most owners want to keep them. However, like any other car, recalls are a part of ownership. Finding EV models with fewer recalls gives you the best of both worlds: Enjoying your vehicle's performance without worrying about safety issues.
